speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been brought to my attention that the statement which I made on April 5 announcing the terms of the fourth victory loan has been misinterpreted. At that tinm I stated that the long term bonds bearing interest at three per cent per annum will mature at par on May 1, 1957, but will be redeemable at the option of the government at par and accrued interest on or after May 1, 1954, at sixty days' notice. This redemption date is provided in the terms of the offering merely as a time after which the government has the option of redeeming or calling the bonds before maturity and paying the holders one hundred cents on each dollar they have invested. Similar callable provisions are to be found in practically all long term government bonds.
This has been misinterpreted to give prevalence to the story that the bonds of the fourth victory loan will not be marketable until after May 1, 1954, which is absolutely incorrect. The bonds of the fourth victory loan will be just as saleable as the bonds of earlier victory loans, which have

had a ready market since their date of issue. Before every victory loan we are deluged with rumours all of which seem to attempt to impair the sale of bonds. The fourth victory loan is no exception. Such rumours are false, vicious and subversive. They could not be worse if they were enemy inspired, which they may be. I urge that Canadians everywhere do everything in their power to stamp out such rumours. I suggest that they inquire into the facts, before repeating stories which are designed to impair the effectiveness of national efforts, such as the fourth victory loan.

Those of us who have made some study of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation's structure realize that it is half and half, so to speak, partly a department of government and partly a public corporation. As I understand, it is m some respects like the Canadian National Railways while in other respects it is not. One of the recommendations of the radio broadcasting committee last year was that this anomalous position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should be clarified, and I hope the government will do something about it.
During the proceedings of the radio broadcasting committee last session, I had occasion to refer in effect to the status of the corporation as an emanation from the crown which has only half emanated. The report of that committee recognized certain anomalies in the status of the corporation and indicated

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: REFERENCE TO NEWSPAPER REFORT OF ACCUMTJLA-LATION OF UNITED STATES EXCHANGE
speechtext:
With the unanimous consent of the committee I should like to make a brief statement. I have been asked to comment on the news dispatch from Washington that Canada may have to take steps to prevent the accumulation of too much United States exchange. It will be recalled that in my budget speech on March 2, I referred to the improvement in our exchange position and stated that shortage of United States dollars had ceased to be a major problem. This improvement was the subject of discussion with the United States treasury shortly after the beginning of the year and again more recently, and an agreement has been reached on the policy to be followed.
It is the case that Canada is in balance with the United States on civilian or nonwar account. In other words, our ordinary exports and other current receipts of United States dollars are sufficient to cover our nonwar requirements. This is the position which Canada has been struggling to reach ever since the start of the war, by economizing in non-essential expenditures of United States dollars. At the moment there is a surplus on non-war account, but the amount involved is extremely small, and I am not in a position to predict whether there will continue to be a surplus throughout the year.
United States dollars required to pay for continuing heavy purchases of war materials and supplies have to be obtained in large measure through sales of other war goods to the United States-the arrangement w'hich was embodied in the Hyde Park agreement. It was not the intention that this arrangement should provide Canada with an amount of United States dollars in excess of our requirements, and I anticipate no technical difficulty in carrying out the principles of the Hyde Park agreement in such a way that, apart from temporary fluctuations, we may avoid building up a large surplus or running into a deficit again.

speechtext: I was unable to make an explanation last night; I shall do so now. Under this resolution employers are required to file an information return on May 31 of thi3 year showing the remuneration paid to persons in their employ in 1942 and also the amount of tax deducted at the source from salary or wages. Prior to the change-over to the pay-as-you-earn basis these returns were not due until October 15, 1943, a date which came after the last deductions in respect of the 1942 tax had been made. If they could see it visually it would help industry considerably and make the workers realize that more of their wages are really theirs than appears to be the case at the end of the week when they get their pay envelope.

I think that is a good suggestion. Several suggestions have been made, and they are being given consideration, with regard to having some form of notice which can be given to the employee in his pay-envelope so that he will have some assurance that part of the sums that are being deducted is to be returned, and some information given as to the form in which it will come back.	_
With regard to the changed date of filing returns, the return itself has printed on it the date when it is to be filed. I do not think there is any doubt that those concerned will know the date the return is due.

Suppose a dozen home owners bn a street employ a man to cut grass and look after the garden, and in the winter fire the boiler, what procedure have those home owners to follow? Are they obliged to make a deduction from what they pay the janitor and remit it to the government, or does the janitor himself have to put in a return indicating what he receives from each?

It depends first on the man's rate of pay. If he is being paid at a taxable rate, that is, $660 for a single man or $1,200 if married, whoever is paying him is supposed to deduct the money at the source and make the return to the government.

How would the home
owner know that? The man may be looking after the homes of ten different owners one month and only four or five another month.

The home owner is not inquiring how much the janitor is making. All he needs to determine is how much he is paying him. If he is paying the janitor a sum that is not taxable then the home owner does
not deduct, although the janitor might be going to several homes and collecting similar amounts from different employers.
Supposing he looks after ten homes and receives from each $5 a month, or $50 from the ten; the home owner would not bother?

That does not follow, because the janitor might be employed only two hours a day.. He might therefore be paid at a rate which if continued throughout the year would make him taxable. It depends on the man's rate of pay whether the deduction must be made.

Suppose I pay a janitor $10 a month for' looking after my home and garden. That would be only $120 a year. That rate would not be taxable. On the other hand he might be working for half a dozen others; I do not know that.
It depends what your arrangement is with him. If he comes to you only two hours a day that might make him taxable.

In order to make it clear for those who hire part-time employees, do I understand that one must decide according to the rate he pays whether the employee would be taxable if employed full time at that rate?
That is right.
And if the employer is paying at a rate which would make the man taxable if employed full time, he must make a deduction and return?
That is right.
Even though the employer knows that the man is not employed full time?
Yes, that is correct.

It puts a responsibility upon a home owner that is confusing both to him and to the employee. A home owner may employ a man one day a week at $6 a day. A single man employed the year round at $6 a day would be taxable. But the home owner, knowing that the man is doing this work only one day a week, in deducting the tax and making a return to the government causes much confusion over a very small matter.

Well, that is what the act says-that if a man is paid at a rate which would make a taxable amount, the home owner must deduct. While he may assume the

man is not working some place else, other people might be wrong in their assumption, and the man might be getting an income from various sources which would require him to pay income tax. That is why the provision is in the act.

Next week I will be letting a number of contracts for papering, painting and carpentering. In each case I get a tender from a painter or paperhanger or carpenter. When the work is finished the bill is presented and I write out a cheque. Do I have to deduct anything from those cheques?
No. In those cases the contractor is not an employee; he is a contractor.

I think the point raised a few moments ago by the leader of the opposition has considerable merit; that is, in regard to the instalments and the dates when they must be paid by taxpayers all across the country. I wonder if hon. members who are present to-day could take a pencil and put down the dates on which payments should be made for 1942 and 1943 and the instalments payable on those dates. It seems to me that right across the country there must be a great deal of confusion in regard to these matters. Would it not be worth while for the department to issue a concise statement in the form of an advertisement setting out clearly the situation with respect to dates and amounts and all other desirable information pertaining to the two years 1942 and 1943? It is true that people may get this information when they get the forms, but in the meantime they are in doubt. It would be exceedingly helpful to the people, and perhaps would aid the victory loan campaign if a definite statement were made by way of advertisement.
The wartime prices and trade board issues little bulletins which go to every house in the country. If the department would place an advertisement in those bulletins it would help a great deal.

I have received
inquiries on two or three occasions with regard to the status of Canadians employed in the construction of airfields in Newfoundland. I understand that for a time deductions were made from their pay in respect of Canadian income tax, and these deductions were later discontinued. Some of these men tell me that they do not know whether they are going to have to pay income tax on all their earnings. Has the minister any information on that point?
IMr. Gibson.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Withholdings were stopped, but the question of taxability is under consideration. It is a very difficult matter for various reasons, and what arrangement will be made in view of all the circumstances has not been finally decided.
It would be quite a hardship on some of these men if at some later time they had to go back and catch up on all these deductions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I realize that.

I asked the minister a question, but I think both he and I lost sight of it. I asked whether or not steps are being taken to acquaint employers of one employee with the necessity of making deductions and filing returns, and whether any penalty is attached if they did not file a return and still there was no bad faith shown.
The income tax department gives publicity to all the changes made in the act, and of course there is a penalty for failure to file a return.
What is the penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be provided in the bill. The penalties are pretty light at the present time, but this is such an important matter that we propose to increase the penalties, and I think provision will be made for some power of remission by the minister. However, that will be dealt with in the bill.

I believe there are still many employers of one person who are not aware that a deduction should be made from the wages of that persor. The department has not done as thorough a job in this connection as it might have done, in view of the bona fide ignorance that exists.

I should like to emphasize what the hon. gentleman has just said, particularly in respect to farmers. I doubt very much whether a great many farmers who employ part-time labour, as farmers do in the summer months for haying and harvesting, know that they should make a deduction and file a return w-ith the government. It seems to me something should be done to acquaint farmers with this provision; otherwise I believe they will be liable to a fine or penalty of some sort.
I bring this to the attention of the minister because I think it is important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This is a very contentious matter that was raised last night and I respectfully submit to the committee that this resolution should be passed. It does not commit the committee to the section I read last night; this is a matter to be dealt with on the bill. All this resolution says is that section 32A of the act 'should be amended to prevent the reduction or avoidance of liability to tax. Resolutions may be pretty general; in fact in years gone by they were very much more general in their terms than they are to-day. If the committee is in favour of the principle of making the provisions of the law stronger for the purpose of preventing the reduction or avoidance of liability to tax; if it is in favour of the principle of doing that by an amendment to section 32A, that is all the committee will be committing itself to by passing this resolution, and then the debate can take place on the section. I read the section last night for the purpose of telling the committee what my intentions were in regard to the amendment of that section. I invited the comments of the committee and I invite them now. If members have any other views as to how we should do this, I should be glad to have them now. They will all be taken into consideration in drafting the section which I shall put before the house.
As I understand it, the actual wording of the resolution was as given a few moments ago by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Section 32A (1) which
appears on page 2226 of Hansard is evidently the section at present in the act, and the following phraseology is that which is to be added as a means of strengthening the provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is not quite correct.
What appears in the middle of the second column of page 2226 of Hansard is the section which I proposed last night as being the appropriate section to put in the act. Section 32A (1) is different from the present 32A (1).

This is not 32A (1) of
the act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. Further consideration will be given to the wording of these provisions in the light of the observations of the committee. What finally is brought before the house can be debated then. I think we should be safe enough in passing the general resolution if the committee is in favour of the principle of amending 32A in some way to prevent the reduction or avoidance of liability to taxation.

I take it that we are
discussing 32A (1) now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are discussing resolution 27, which provides that section 32A of the act be amended to prevent the reduction or avoidance of liability to tax.

Since last evening we
have had an opportunity of studying the proposed amendment. There would appear to be a typographical error in section 32A (1) as it appears on page 2226 of Hansard. I take it that the word "as" in line four should be "has."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I propose to confine my
remarks principally to the first subsection. This subsection gives to the treasury board the task of determining the extent to which taxation under the act has been or, but for the application of this section, would be avoided, reduced or prejudiced thereby and in accordance with such determination there shall be assessed and levied upon such taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct and such tax shall be payable by him as in this act provided. It seems to me that that is a very considerable power to give to the treasury board.
Too much.

I have not changed my
opinion that this will not offend the great charters of mankind, but we must realize that income tax has been extended considerably, not only as regards the amount of the tax imposed but as to the numbers of individuals to which it applies. This tax now takes in a much greater number of the citizens of substance and it goes down into the fairly low income brackets. I think this committee and the minister should be extremely careful in enacting any amendment that would permit any injustice or inequity in the application of this particular act.
Just for a moment I should like to refer to the act itself and recall to the committee the general provision having to do with appeals by the taxpayer. At the present time if a taxpayer is dissatisfied with his assessment he may appeal to the minister. As defined in the act that would be the Minister of National Revenue. Under the act the minister is charged with the duty of reviewing the assessment and he must then notify the taxpayer whether he sustains the judgment of the commissioner of income tax or whether he amends it. If the taxpayer is still dissatisfied, he has the right of appeal to the exchequer court.
Income War Tax

In theory that would appear to be a fairly safe and fair provision for the taxpayer, but I submit that in the light of my own experience, and I am sure in the light of the experience of many lawyers who have had occasion to represent clients who have taken advantage of this provision, the minister has not discharged and cannot in the very nature of the circumstances discharge this duty himself. The minister cannot possibly take the time and trouble to review the application of the taxpayer, he must delegate that task to some departmental officer.
The trouble with this type of tribunal is that there is a partnership in interest between the commissioner of income tax, whose duty it is to give a decision on the assessment and the amount of taxation payable thereon, and the person to whom the appeal is made. The minister could discharge this task I presume with a large degree of fairness, but because of the similarity of interests, because of this partnership of employment as it were, the result of the usual procedure is likely to be to make the taxpayer feel that he has not been fairly dealt with. My own experience has been that only on a very few occasions has a minister ever attempted to change a decision of the commissioner of income tax. The commissioner is a very able man familiar with the provisions and the decisions of the courts thereon, and the minister would be loath to take upon himself the duty of changing a decision of this responsible officer of the crown.
As I have pointed out, there is now the right of appeal from the minister to the court, but under this section 32A it will be noted that there is no appeal to the minister; the appeal is direct to the exchequer court. Here of course you will get an independence of judgment by the tribunal charged with trying the case, as it were. It may be suggested that that should satisfy all the requirements, but I would call the attention of the minister to the fact that very few citizens, apart from the wealthy corporations or the wealthy individuals who employ lawyers as a matter of course and who enter upon litigation with a certain degree of familiarity, will be inclined to take advantage of the right of appeal granted under this particular section. The vast majority of taxpayers will hesitate before appealing a decision of an officer of the government to the exchequer court.
He would not be able to finance an appeal.

The cost is great and the trouble is considerable. As a matter of fact, he just will not do it. The average sensible

lawyer now does not try to persuade his client to enter upon this course. If we are to delegate to some agency of government the power to administer acts of this house, then the tribunal or body which passes judgment upon the fairness or unfairness of decisions of an officer of the crown should be independent. Incidentally this is an example of the necessity of always keeping in mind the need to keep our judiciary separate and apart and independent of all conflicting interests and controversies. The judiciary are subject to income tax, and being human they form opinions and prejudices about the fairness or unfairness of the income tax act. In the interests, not of the judges, but of the people of this country whom the judiciary serve, we should be wise to keep in mind the British principle which puts the judiciary in a position of complete independence of interest in all matters that agitate the minds of the citizens whose cases they have to try. I realize that this is a difficult problem to solve but I am thoroughly in agreement with the minister that we must find some remedy for the evil of companies and perhaps individuals seeking to evade the tax laws of this country.
It is not evasion but avoidance.

It is really a method of evasion. Taking advantage of all the loopholes that appear in the act, corporations and individuals, serving their own interests, will resort' to all sorts of subterfuges to escape the impositions of the act. However, in setting up a remedy this house does not want to alienate the sympathy which we should invite from the taxpayers for the act itself.
I would make two suggestions. I appreciate that one of them may not be workable. One suggestion would be that if the treasury board is to assume this duty, some person with long judicial or legal experience who is peculiarly well fitted to deal with taxation matters be invited to sit in with the treasury board, and. unless he approves the decision reached, let the matter be referred to, let us say, the exchequer court. I think we must try to avoid litigation on the part of the taxpayer. I do not think we shall find a solution that will satisfy the taxpayer if we provide only a path that leads to costly legal disputes. An appeal 'to the exchequer court should be considered only as a last resort for those who feel strongly about the decision reached. I should like to see some independent body, free from interest either as a taxing authority or as an interested taxpayer, empowered to

Income War Tax
consider all the facts and reach a decision which both the government and the taxpayer could feel was an equitable and fair decision.
My other suggestion is one that I submit for consideration with a little more confidence. It might be wise to take this duty away from the treasury board altogether and to free the minister of the duty of reviewing the taxpayer's complaint. Let that matter be given to a body of three persons, independent of government and independent, so far as that is possible, of the taxpayer. Perhaps that body should have upon it a chartered accountant, because in many ways chartered accountants are more capable-
That would be another board.

I know it, and it might mean added expense. I do not like that, but we have a difficult task here, and to accomplish our purpose we must see that it is done in a way that will intelligently invite the support of the taxpayer.
How can you succeed unless you are prepared to acknowledge that the body to deal with it is the exchequer court?

I was going to suggest this, and it is only a suggestion because I have not had time to think it through. I suggest that the treasury board discharge that first duty because they have officers who are in possession of all the facts and are able to form a shrewd practical judgment on taxing matters. It is only natural that they become a little cynical of mankind and suspect, a little more than the judiciary would, the taxpayer who is seeking to get redress or relief from taxation. It is only natural that these officers of the crown should become hardened in their attitude towards complaints that are not well justified. Let the treasury board discharge this first duty, but before their decision becomes operative, let it be reviewed by a body of three, including a judge, a chartered accountant and an ordinary business man-representing the citizen's point of view.
Such a board would give the taxpayer a sense of his case having been reviewed independently and without bias. If after the decision of that body had been given the taxpayer still feels a sense of wrong, let him have the right of appeal to the exchequer court. As it now stands, too much power and too much responsibility is given to the treasury board, and it will make them a very unpopular body in this country.
Turning to the phraseology of the first section I notice it provides that the treasury
board shall not only assess but levy upon a taxpayer such tax as the board may direct. There is nothing there imposing a limit on the tax which the board may impose. The wording is:
There shall be assessed and levied upon any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct.
That applies not only to the assessment but to the levying of the tax. That is unlimited power to give to any body.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am inclined to agree.

Some phraseology should be introduced to alter that. The amount of income having been determined, it should be subject to the rates of taxation prescribed by the act.
These are only suggestions. I am fully in favour of finding some remedy for this evil, and it is only a matter of giving it proper consideration and working out the most sensible and practical method.

This problem must have been the subject of legislation in Great Britain. Has the minister given any consideration to their legislation covering this point? Many of these cases are paralleled by similar cases in other countries. In view of the situation which developed in the debate yesterday and again to-day I think most members have the fear that the principle involved is a bad one. I realize that those who listen to a debate such as this may think that small things are being magnified.
The difficulty as I see it-I do not speak as an expert on this kind of legislation, but simply from the common sense point of view- is that legislation such as this might form a dangerous and perilous precedent in the future. That was pretty well covered in the debate yesterday, and I have no desire to reiterate the arguments made then, except to say that this legislation would provide an opportunity for the thin end of the wedge to be worked in so far as taxation is concerned. This parliament of 245 men and women gathered from all over Canada have one weapon by which the rights of the citizens can be safeguarded, and that is the granting of supply and the raising of taxation. It seems to me that if this principle is endorsed by parliament there is a real danger of its being the first block or cornerstone in the building up of something that we in Canada do not want to see built. That is putting it very simply; I am not attempting to argue from the point of view of legal definitions or from any especially complicated constitutional point, of view, even were I capable of doing it. When you place the matter of levying taxation in the hands oi

Income War Tax
some body other than parliament, you adopt a principle which may quite properly be regarded in a democracy as a retrograde constitutional step.
I do not want to be put in the light of raising an unnecessary difficulty for the minister. I know what his desire is; I think I know the objective to which he is moving. But in attempting to gain it we had better stop, look and listen. This parliament should be sure that in moving toward one objective we are not abandoning some safeguard which means far more to parliament than any amount of taxation that might be collected. [DOT]
I believe the minister will recognize, from what was said yesterday and what may yet be said, the dangers which lurk in a course which does not appear to have full constitutional and legal justification.
I would like some information from the minister as to how the United Kingdom handles matters of this kind. British experience would provide, I should suppose, precedents which would be useful to us in this house. Before this is incorporated in the bill or before the bill is passed, I suggest that he carefully canvass and skilfully explore such avenues as are open to us in the example and experience of other parts of the world, so that, before we launch on what may be a dangerous course, we shall draw upon the wisdom and the parallel experience of others.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In Great Britain the problem is not nearly so acute, for this reason: properly speaking, there is no corporation income tax in the United Kingdom. The corporation income is taxed in the hands of the corporation but is credited to the individual shareholder. If the income upon receipt by the corporation is taxed at 50 per cent, then, when it goes out to the shareholder, he may find that his tax on it is already fully paid.
Or more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or more than paid, or perhaps only slightly less than paid. Therefore the incentive is very much less than it is in this country.
It is a fairer system.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With regard to the British statutes, several of the phrases which are used in these amendments, such as "artificially reduced", "artificially reduce", and "main purpose", are taken from those statutes. With regard to the procedure and the tribunals I am unable to give my hon. friend any definite information. I am under the impression that they have commissioners, functioning somewhat in the nature of tax courts, who pass on these matters.
Do they have laymen as members of these committees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot give the committee any definite information.
I think they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In the United States, of course, they have the same system of taxation as we have. That is, they have the corporation tax, and then upon distribution of the profits of the corporation to the shareholders, the shareholders are themselves taxed. I assume it was because of this problem that a few years ago they placed a tax upon undistributed surplus, wThich caused a tremendous storm in the United States and was, I think, finally repealed, because it had detrimental effects which were considered sufficient to outweigh the beneficial effects. What they do at the present time I do not know
I am inclined to agree that the provision in the act of 1940, which we carried into this act, but which we did not originate in this act, about taxation being imposed in such sum as the treasury board may direct, is objectionable. The new subsections do not contain that.-that is, subsection 2 and subsection 3- and I certainly will give serious consideration to changing that provision of subsection 1. When the hon. gentleman speaks about the dangers of creating a precedent which may be used to oppress the individual, there is something to be said for that.
We have to be jealous of those rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes; there is something to be said for that. But there is another danger which concerns me very much. I think that the present economic system, all things considered, is a better one than some others which have been suggested.
The minister would not have any in mind, I suppose?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I do not want to get
into a controversy here. But, whatever jealousy< parliament may have of the rights of the individual, parliament has to make sure that this economic system functions cleanly and justly and fairly, to the extent of its ability. I have perhaps given an impression that the practices I mentioned last night are widespread. I do not think they are. But a few instances, known by a few individuals and passed from mouth to mouth, of skilful and wealthy individuals who legally are able to escape the clear spirit and intent of taxation legislation, will do more to discredit the system we live under and more

Income War Tax
to discredit the parliament that did not have the foresight to prevent these things, than almost anything you can think of; and I have come to the conclusion that we ought to strain a point here. We are at war. It may be that this would not be as necessary in time of peace. But it would worry me a great deal if I heard of an instance here and an instance there of persons withdrawing large sums, and the sums we are thinking of here are large sums, running sometimes into the hundreds of thousands or possibly millions of dollars, and being able to get this money without payment of tax, contrary to the true spirit and intent of the act. I ask the hon. gentleman, who comes in contact with people who have experience in these things and who are in the business world, to inquire of them what they think can be done under the present act, and if they have ever heard of any cases of its being done. I think he will be surprised. The commissioner of income tax, of course, watches these surpluses; and if he sees them coming down he knows something is going on. Sometimes the business purpose is in evidence. It is a legitimate business purpose, and should not be interfered with. Sometimes there is no legitimate business purpose, and it is purely a scheme to avoid taxation, under circumstances where there is no real, moral justification for the avoidance of the tax.
In the Victorian period the avoidance of taxation was a polite, gentlemanly game. Taxation was low, and if a taxpayer could find a hole in the law and crawl through it, everyone laughed about it and tried to block up the hole. But it did not make very much difference.

Or tried to get through
the hole.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the crown could prevent his finding a hole, they would not get away with it. There was no moral interest involved. But when taxation becomes as heavy as it is to-day, when to a very great extent the people of this country are working for the state-and properly working for the state -then it is not an amusing matter, and is beyond the realm of a game. It becomes something-well, perhaps not exactly treason, but something considered most unpatriotic and unsocial.
Last night the hon. member asked why it should not be made a crime. I said I did not think a section could be drafted so as to accomplish anything. For instance if under this section we were to make evasion a crime, every hon. member in the committee
would say that the mere effort of trying to do that is a crime. The definition would be so loose that we should be bound to sweep in some transactions which are perfectly legitimate, and the result would be that we should not get convictions. The crown would have to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt. The position taken last night was: Do not make them pay, but make them suffer. This is to make them pay that which it is their intention to avoid paying. That is what I am tiying to do in the present instance. I am trying to plug up loopholes for evasion, and I am doing it in the only way I know how to do it.
As I have said, if we make it as definite as we ought to make it for the guidance of a court we will be so definite that other ways will be found to get around it. Therefore it must be pretty wide, and there must be some discretionary powers in the tribunal making the decision. We have vested discretionary powers in a committee of a committee of parliament. That is really what the treasury board is. It is in fact a committee of the cabinet which, in turn, is a committee of parliament. It seems to me that that would be the appropriate tribunal.
If we were to take the suggestion of the hon. member for Swift Current and set up a board, such board would be a court. The court would have power to a very large extent to make its own law and create its own jurisdiction.
All courts have that power; jnitial .law-making goes on every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But within a much narrower limit than wrould 'be the case here.

I see what the minister is trying to do. There seem to be .two things involved in this amendment. The first is an attempt to prevent-and I will use the word- evasion of taxation imposed by parliament. That is something we are all interested in seeing done. We want to prevent anything approaching an evasion of legitimate obligations under the law. The difficulty then appears to be that certain powers have to be given to some body to make some decision, and that those powers have to be blanket powers. When I heard this read last night-and like many other hon. members I was not- familiar with it before last night; I do not know just how it got on the statute book, because I had not looked it up-I was surprised at the implications involved. But there are so many items passing through parliament that we simply cannot keep in-
Income War Tax

formed with respect .to all of them. I confess that I cannot, because I have not sufficient staff to do it. To my mind the objectionable words were "levied upon any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board- may direct." That is the objectionable phraseology.
The intention may be entirely different from the meaning conveyed by those words, but it leaves the possibility of a wide interpretation which, as I said- last night, in my opinion is contrary to the fundamental basis of our .parliamentary government, that the representatives of the people in parliament assembled shall have the sole right to levy taxes. That is the age-old struggle parliament had with the crown, and we may actually find ourselves in a position of .parliament struggling with a government. I am not referring to this government, but use the term in the broad sense. We may find parliament struggling with a government to retain control in parliament, when a government attempts to usurp that power.
While I should be the last one in the house to endeavour to prevent the imposition of taxation on corporations, and particularly corporations which are trying to evade their just dues to the people of Canada, nevertheless I feel that even where a corporation is involved one would be less than fair if he did not see what I believe to be the implications behind this phraseology.
I like the suggestion of the hon. member for Swift Current, that some commission be set up. The minister suggested that he believed a commission having certain' powers has been established in Great Britain. I have a hazy idea that that is so, and that there is some commission to which they may appeal in Great Britain. But I like the suggestion of the hon. member for Swift Current that there be established a body with judicial powers to which appeal might be made both by the government or its officials, and by the person or the corporation.
What I dislike about the proposed legislation is that one of the litigants, if I may use the term, is also the judge. It seems to me that that is a bad principle in law, apart altogether from the other side of the matter which I have emphasized in my earlier remarks. In my view the body making the decision with respect to taxation ought to be independent, and ought not to be interested in the results of any appeal.
The wording of this amendment is so wide that it actually gives a committee not directly responsible to the house, but directly responsible to another committee which is responsible to the house-the cabinet-powers, in the 
phraseology of the amendment, to levy "upon any taxpayer such tax as the treasury board may direct, and such tax shall be payable by him as in this act provided." That is what I regard as objectionable. I should like to see some method of getting around it.

There are two sections to be considered here, I think, sections 32A and 32A(1). As the hon. member Mr. Coldwell has said, this is a very objectionable way of raising a tax. I suggest that the wording of both these sections be reconsidered. I have not attempted to redraft them, but it seems to me that if we were to provide something to this effect, that where a person transfers property for the purpose of reducing or avoiding taxation he shall be liable to be taxed on such property in an amount equal to the amount of the tax that he attempted to evade, then the responsibility is not on the treasury board; it is on the minister, and he can impose the tax on the person or company which is endeavouring to avoid it. If the company or person thinks an injustice is being done he has the- right to appeal to the exchequer court as the act provides. I suggest that something of this kind be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes-thank you.

This is peculiarly a point for those in the legal profession, but from the point of view of one engaged in business may I try to indicate how it strikes me. First I was interested in what the minister said in regard to the economic system under which we operate; it must undoubtedly be kept clean and wholesome and the spirit of competition must be allowed play. Certainly no greater resentment can be felt than by those who are heavy taxpayers against those who leave Canada for the purpose of decreasing the amount of tax they have to pay, because it means that those of us who choose to stay in Canada- and most of us fortunately do-have a greater amount to pay. So that there can be no sympathy with the class who are seeking to evade taxes.
On the other hand if the minister wishes to keep this system of ours wholesome, I hope the government will do its part also. If it would allow the salaries of some of the government officials to be published, such as those ini the Bank of Canada and the Canadian National Railways which were refused in the committee the other day, I think it would be a salutary step. The salaries of corporation officials as a group are published under our company law, and in the United States individually. There is no reason for keeping these matters from the public whose money

Income War Tax
they receive. The Canadian National Railways intimate that they do not wish to publish the salaries because of competition; in the case of the Bank of Canada there is no such reason.
Would the hon. member go all the way and have the salaries of the officials of all corporations published?

Yes, I think any corporation should publish the salaries of its officials. In that regard I may not find complete agreement on the part of some officials; nevertheless the money belongs to the shareholders and I see no reason why the salaries of officers of public companies should not be published.
I believe hon. members felt last night when original section 32A was read that this was an invasion of the rights of the citizen as against the crown, and many hon. members,
I think, were surprised that that section did exist. Now the minister wishes greatly to enlarge the force and scope of the section so that there shall be no loophole. I do not think so much objection would be taken if the minister would bring down legislation to stop up a particular loophole or set of loopholes. But no; this draft amendment is asking not only to block loopholes of which he may know, but to go into other cases which may come up in the future.
The minister has said that taxation has taken on quite a different aspect, partly because of the present crucial emergency, and partly because of the high rates of taxation that go with it. It is no longer a game where a good solicitor can drive a coach and four through any 'act of parliament. Nevertheless, as he inferentially pointed out, the situation in this country' is conducive to lawyers using legal methods to assist clients in evading taxation, and while I do not wish to open up the whole field of corporation, taxes, the minister himself has said that the need for such prying legislation as he is asking for, remedial legislation, does not exist in Great Britain because they do not have these corporation taxes. I do not wish to say they are iniquitous but they seem unfair inasmuch as corporations can neither eat nor drink nor otherwise use the income but are merely trustees for the people who put in their capital and thus create jobs for the people. There is no reason why the same money should be taxed twice and in some cases three times.
Perhaps another reason why the minister finds the difficulty more acute at the present time than under ordinary circumstances is that a surplus might have been accumulated for legitimate needs, but the company may
have changed its type of business or may now find itself pretty much a holding company with a large earned surplus. When that surplus was accumulated perhaps ten or twenty years ago the rate of tax on the individuals who really owned it might have been five or ten or fifteen per cent, but now the incidence of tax on the people who own the company and who would receive the money is perhaps sixty or seventy or eighty per cent. So that the minister must realize that while to some extent there is a moral issue at stake, the crown itself has brought about a set of conditions which lead to getting around the tax if it can be done legally. A business man must know where he stands. I am sure the minister will recall the old legal maxim that it is better that the law' should be certain than that it should be just. You cannot go on doing business unless you know where you stand. While a set of rules may be exercised fairly and judicially by one administration, there may be at some time a subsequent administration operating those rules in such a way that it will be absolutely impossible for business to carry on. This brings me back to the fact that if the minister would suggest legislation for particular cases I think the committee would receive it much more favourably than to ask for such blanket powers as he is seeking under this section.
I might refer briefly to the position of the subject as against the crown. People perhaps get the impression that this is all onesided, that there are iniquitous people lying awake nights trying with the help of able counsel to do the crown out of some of its just dues. But I tell the minister that the crown is just as unfair and iniquitous and sets a worse example than individuals.

"The king can do no
wrong".
That is a legal theory.

Some of his advisers
can.

Unfortunately there are too many "kings" in this country. That brings me to the point of succession duties. Just let me tell the committee, and perhaps particularly my hon. friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, that if a person in either the great province of Quebec or the great province of Ontario dies while holding as an asset a share in a company whose head office is in the other province, then his estate must pay a full tax on that share in Ontario, a full tax in Quebec and a full tax to the dominion. There is no equity as between the crown and the individual in many cases, and
Income War Tax

in view of the high taxes that exist at the present time the crown is getting many windfalls from income which was earned in previous years when the rates of taxation were only a fraction of what they are to-day, but which income is only now being paid out. For instance, I will mention executors' fees. An executor may work on an estate for five or ten years and receive little or nothing until a final settlement is made. If he asks for that settlement to-day, or if by reason of his. death the settlement is made to-day, the crown applies the tax on the money which he made back in 1935, or prior to that time, but at the rates of taxation which are applicable to-day.
I just want to point out to the minister that the matter is not entirely one-sided, that no law can be made to operate with exact fairness under all circumstances; and while we must do all we can to prevent evasions of taxation, nevertheless the crown does make up on some items what it loses on others. The essential point, is, I believe, that if you cannot draft specific- legislation to prevent evasions, then if the liberty of the individual is to be jeopardized by a blanket amendment such as is proposed, the crown must forfeit its right. Otherwise it means that the state is put ahead of the individual, which is in essence the whole theory of totalitarianism.
As I have mentioned, however, the whole question is one for corporation and constitutional lawyers who must look after the rights of the individual, and who have knowledge of the principles which apply. I am sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his seat at the moment, because I should like to ask an opinion from him as to whether or not he thinks the rights of the citizens of this great country are protected under the suggested amendment; for, after all, he is to a large extent the protector and custodian of the rights of the Canadian people.

I have not the income tax act before me, but I seem to remember a provision somewhere in it that if a person does not keep books, for example, the minister may assess the amount of income tax payable. In that case is there any appeal by the person who is assessed from the decision of the minister to a tribunal?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Y es; there is, I feel certain, an appeal provided to the exchequer court. The usual procedure is an assessment by the commissioner and then an appeal to the minister, which almost invariably results in confirmation of the commissioner's assessment; then there is the appeal to the exchequer 
court. Is there something in regard to this about which I do not know? Is that the hon. gentleman's question?

I was going to follow that up by asking why the minister would not be in the same position with regard to this matter as he would be with regard to the person who does not keep books. Therefore why not leave the minister the discretion he has in the other case and permit the same procedure that now exists under the income tax act with regard to appeal? That more or less follows what the hon. member for St. John-Albert said, and I am tempted to support his remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see any section which provides that the minister has any extraordinary power by virtue of the fact that the taxpayer does not keep books. There is a provision that if a taxpayer fails or refuses to keep adequate books or accounts for income tax purposes, the minister may require the taxpayer to keep such records or accounts as he may prescribe.
What happens if he does not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, I do not know; I suppose he would be subject to a penalty.' The fact is that assessments are made fairly arbitrarily at times, because the department simply cannot get any information and they have the power to make assessments. They have to be arbitrary; otherwise they cannot get anywhere; there is just nothing to be done. They have to do the best they can; and, as the bon. gentleman says, that is not very much different from the power of treasury board here. We did not think, perhaps, that these powers should be vested in the minister, because they are extraordinary powers, and it was some protection to say that they should be exercised by the treasury board, which is a committee composed of six ministers.
Though I am in a hurry I think I will place on record some excerpts from articles appearing on the subject of tax avoidance in war time which appeared in the English tax magazine Taxation. I wish these might be read outside this house as well as inside.
Does the minister think there are more offenders outside than in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The excerpts are as follows:
Methods of escape from taxation have exercised the wits of man since the raising of revenue for the public welfare was first put into operation and have taken many forms, from the smuggling of excisable goods to the execution of annuity deeds in favour of children. . . .

Income War Tax
Lord Blackburn, in Coltness Iron Foundry v. Black, said, "No tax can be imposed on the subject without words in an act of parliament clearly showing an intention of laying a burden on him. But when that intention is sufficiently shown, it is, I think, vain to speculate on what would be the fairest and most equitable mode of levying that tax." . . .
In war time few things can be viewed in the same light as in peace time, and the question of legal avoidance of taxation obligations is, in our opinion, one of the foremost of these things. . . .
When, at last, this nightmare of war has passed, we may revert to our former opinion as to the rights of the taxpayer, but so long as our country is fighting for its very existence, we hold the view that the moral liability of the citizen comes before all else. . . .
Time and again, before the commencement of hostilities, eminent judges were at pains to make it crystal clear that it was open to all taxpayers so to arrange their affairs that the amount of tax which might be extracted from them by the revenue authorities was as small as possible. . . .
To-day, when the country is in the throes of the greatest war in its history, we believe that it is the duty of every citizen to pay the full measure of all taxation according to the circumstances in which it finds him when it is imposed. . . .
The legal liability of the taxpayer has given place to the moral liability; a moral liability which is without parallel in the history of taxation. . . .
... in this, the greatest test our country has been called upon to face, the old dicta of learned judges, to the effect that a man is entitled to arrange his affairs to avoid taxation, could not apply. We felt, and we still feel, that the taxpayer's undertakings should bear the burdens imposed by the legislature as those burdens find them. . . .
I place that on record merely because it is of interest, and in order to provoke thought in the minds of citizens generally. I must say I do not see very much in those excerpts with which to disagree.

In line 8, subsection 2 of section 32A it states:
. . . any person subsequent to the year 1939 as a result of such transaction or transactions has been received directly or indirectly from a company having undistributed income on hand. . . .
That goes back four years; but if this is placed upon the statute books to-day, perhaps four or live years from now the income tax division will come along and will then be able to go back eight years. In that way they might be able to take money from a person who had spent what he had received in this way. I think the date is wrong; it should go back not more than four years. Four years should be the limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We went back to the beginning of the war.

That is all right; but if this is on the statute books for another four years, it will mean it will go back eight years and that is rather far-reaching. Supposing the minister received from a company some income which he thought was a legitimate dividend and the commissioner of income tax said it was not, that he was taxable-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would be taxable if it were dividends.
Supposing it were something that the minister thought was legitimate. I think a clause should be inserted limiting it to four years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will give the matter
consideration.

One question by the hon. member for Rosedale which the minister did not answer was in connection with the draftsmanship of this particular section. Was the Minister of Justice or the Department of Justice consulted? It seems to me that if there ever were a need for reference to the Department of Justice, this is it. I do not know how busy that department is, but I do not think it is too busy to give some consideration to a constitutional matter as important as this one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think the Department of Justice has been consulted, but the bill has not yet been prepared.
I wish to make our position clear with respect to the whole matter. We have a resolution in the form of a notice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has been passed by council. I have the authority of the government to propose this.

I have never had the
honour and privilege of being present at council, but I imagine that while the word of the minister may not be taken as absolutely final it has an influential effect upon the decision reached. Perhaps, if I may pay a compliment to the minister, I think his word would carry very considerable weight. This is one instance in which the Minister of Justice and the Department of Justice should have been consulted. This is a constitutional matter and they should have been consulted. I may be entirely wrong in my premise; but I contend that the Minister of Justice should have been asked to give an opinion on the constitutional and legal aspect, entirely apart from the problem of taxation or the avoidance of taxation. Now that the Minister of National Defence is looking my way, may I say that it
Income War Tax

would not have hurt matters if he had been consulted. Sitting together on the front benches opposite are two men who have the reputation of being highly skilled in legal matters. I think this is one instance where the committee, in attempting to find a solution for this problem in collaboration with the minister, should have had the benefit of the expert advice of the Minister of Justice and his department.

Resolution agreed to.
24. That members of the Canadian naval, military and air forces in the Canadian active service forces and in receipt of service pay and allowances in excess of $1,600 shall be allowed a credit from the tax otherwise payable equal to the tax payable on $1,600 (increased by dependents' allowances in the case of married persons but not including any allowance for more than six children) provided that on incomes over $1,600 (or appropriately increased by dependents' allowances) the tax credit shall be reduced in the same proportion that such income exceeds $1,600 (or appropriately increased by dependents' allowances); provided that in the case of female members of the said forces the figure of $1,600 shall be replaced by such appropriate lesser amount as may be determined by the governor in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I so move.
Are nurses on active service not included?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They would be included in members of the Canadian naval, military and air forces. I understand that their pay is commensurate with that received by the men. Let me explain the scheme. Before we introduced the changes last year it was found that a number of ranks in the armed forces, particularly warrant officers, were receiving a net income after taxation greater than that received by the lower commissioned officers.
Mr. JACKMAN; Up to the rank of major.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That- was detrimental to the military organization, because in some instances promotions which should have been made were resisted. The persons did not want to accept the promotions. In order to overcome this problem last year, we said that the tax shall not reduce the net income of any officer below $1,600. That amount was as near as we could come to the pay of a warrant officer. Some warrant officers get a little more than that without trades pay, particularly in the navy, but in the army and air force they get less than $1,600. The provision that the tax should not reduce the net income below $1,600 did away with the anomaly that existed at the time, that the commissioned officer had less money in his pocket after paying the tax than the noncommissioned officer without trades pay.
The trouble with what we did last year was that it left some commissioned officers in the lower ranks receiving the same as the high non-commissioned officers without trades pay. That was undesirable because it left a flat level there. While it did not take money out of the person's pocket to be promoted, it did not give him any more money. It was not a proper gradation of pay. This is designed to remove that anomaly, and so far as we can make a fair provision this is a completely fair provision. Instead of drawing the line between taxable and non-taxable members of the forces, between commissioned and non-commissioned officers, we draw it at $1,600. This means that certain warrant officers, those getting trades pay, who have not heretofore been taxable, will hereafter be taxable to some extent. But it substitutes a rational and logical line or division for a very illogical one. It draws the line on the basis , of pay instead of on the basis of rank.
It does another thing. It provides that, whether he be commissioned or non-commissioned, a single member of the forces who has no dependents and is receiving $1,600 gets

Income War Tax
a credit of the tax on $1,600 against his tax, which means that he pays nothing. As his pay rises there is a proportionate reduction in that tax credit. If his pay rises to $1,700 there is a one-sixteenth reduction of his tax credit; at $1,800 there is a reduction of two-sixteenths of the tax credit; at $1,900 there is a reduction of three-sixteenths, and so on until at $3,200 there is a sixteen-sixteenth reduction of the tax credit, or, in other words, no tax credit at all.
The application of the formula will mean that a person in receipt of army pay higher than that of another member of the forces will always have more left to him after paying his tax. There would be an even gradation of his net income between $1,600 and $3,200. At $3,200 the tax credit disappears altogether. Commissioned officers resident in Canada are fully taxable on their pay if it is in excess of $3,200 and if they are single.
These figures of $1,600 and $3,200 become altered very greatly in the case of those having wives and children. The figure for a married) person without children is $2,100. instead of $1,600; for a married person with one child it is $2,255, and for a married person with two children, $2,400. That alters the scale of tax credits.
This increase in exemptions, so to speak, of the married person, of the married person with one child, of the married person with two children or more, involves as its necessary corollary a tax on dependents' allowance. The dependents' allowance has been regarded since	the beginning	of the	war as taxableas against the member of the forces, and we intend to continue it as taxable, and in fact to confirm what we have been doing. It would completely upset our whole system if there were any question about that fact. Accordingly that will be done in another resolution. He gets	this	concession,	thishigher floor, this allowance of his tax by reason of having a wife, and a further allowance	by reason of having	one child,	twochildren, and so on. It follows, we think, that on that scheme of things the dependents' allowance should be taxable. They always have	been taxable.	The	Department	of
Justice gave an opinion at the beginning of the war that they were taxable.
The question was referred to the justice department?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, at the outset of the war. Of course., it is income; by virtue of the man's employment with the crown the allowance goes to his wife and to his children. What I am pointing out is that the taxing
of the dependents' allowance is necessarily involved in this plan of rising floors, and on that account the allowance is taxable.
This does not apply to members of the forces whose duties are performed outside Canada, afloat or in aircraft, as in resolution 22.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that is not changed. There is no extension there, and no extension to those serving overseas.
No tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No tax.

speechtext:
I do not blame the hon. member for asking the question. There was a lot to do. You cannot get your drafting

done with strict accuracy in a hurry, and when you have to rise in the house and defend it line by line and word by word you read it fairly carefully. It was obvious upon consideration that the other resolution was not accurate, and this one is.

Can the situation arise where a member of the forces drawing $1,600 a year would find, after he paid his tax, that he would have a net amount left which was less than what a member of the forces drawing $1,550 received?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Just a matter of explanation of this dependents' allowance business. It has been, as the minister knows, a great bone of contention to the armed services. I will point out one case in which, it may seem, I am interested. No member of the armed forces who is also a member of the house draws dependents' allowance; you cannot draw allowances from two sources at the same time. I wish to make that clear. As I understand it, at the present time an unmarried officer is given tax exemption up to $1,600 of his army pay. Am I correct in that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Under this proposal?
Under this proposal, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If he gets under $1,600 he is exempted on the entire amount; if he gets over $1,600 he is taxable and gets a tax credit of the tax on $1,600.
That is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Subject to a slight reduction the higher he goes.
If he gets $1,700 his reduction is fifteen-sixteenths, and on $1,800 it is fourteen-sixteenths?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Two-sixteenths.
Two-sixteenths, yes. His exemption is reduced one-sixteenth for every $100 over $1,600?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Right.
For your married officer the exemption starts at $2,250, or $2,150?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A married person without children, at $2,100.
That is tantamount to allowing the married officer a further exemption of $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. What happens there is that the married officer runs from $2,100 to $4,200.
Yes, but he does not begin to pay taxes until his army pay and dependents' allowances come to $2,100?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.
Therefore it comes to almost the same thing as allowing that officer $500 exemption on his dependents' allowance, because the unmarried officer gets no dependents' allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, yes, I think that is substantially correct. These words are tricky. It may not be exactly the same. That is the principle of it, and I think that is right.

I think that is a good principle. I commend the minister for it, because the married officer has definitely suffered a hardship in being taxed on his dependents' allowance. Many cases have been made in support of the contention that the taxation on dependents' allowance is an unsound premise. I know the government have always taxed the dependents' allowance. I think it is unsound. Of course, an officer serving overseas is not taxed on his pay or on his dependents' allowance. When both husband and wife are living in Canada, both have the same expenses. I think it can be shown and reasonably argued that the dependent living in Canada, whether or not the member of the armed forces is serving overseas or in this country, still has to live and has to provide for the same amount of expenses irrespective of where her next of kin is serving.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The discrimination there
arises from our discrimination in favour of officers overseas.
Yes, to a certain extent it does. But if the dependents' allowance were tax-free, that discrimination against the dependent would not occur.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would not be as great; that is all.
This, I think, is a step in the right direction. I should like to see it carried further, but it certainly will help in the case I have mentioned.

22. That the service pay and allowances of the Canadian naval, military and air forces while in the Canadian active service forces in the western hemisphere other than in Canada shall be subject to income tax at one-half the effective rate applicable to each individual taxpayer, such rate to be determined by calculating the total tax on each taxpayer's total income, determining the effective rate which the tax bears to such total income and allowing a credit against the tax payable of one-half of the effective rate on such service pay and allowances; provided, however, that no tax shall be payable in respect of the service pay and allowances of any such member of the Canadian naval, military and air forces whose total service pay does not
exceed the sum of $1,600 (or in the case of female members of the said services such lower appropriate amount as shall be determined by the governor in council) and provided further that no tax shall be payable on service pay and allowances by members of the said forces whose duties are of such a character as are required normally to be performed afloat or in aircraft.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move the following amendment :
That the resolution be amended by substituting therefor the following:
"22. That the service pay and allowances of the Canadian naval, military and air forces while in the Canadian active service forces in the western hemisphere other than in Canada shall be subject to income tax at one-half the effective rate applicable to each individual taxpayer, such rate to be determined by calculating the total tax on each taxpayer's total income, determining the effective rate which the tax bears to such total income and allowing a credit against the tax payable of one-half of the effective rate on such service pay and allowances; provided, however, that the exemptions and tax credits for members of the armed forces as provided for in resolution 24 hereof shall apply pro tanto to members of the forces affected by this resolution; provided further that no tax shall be payable on service pay and allowances by members of the said forces whose duties are of such a character as are required normally to be performed afloat or in aircraft."
This is simply a matter of rewording, and correcting certain inaccuracies. The effect of the resolution, however, is exactly the same. It is to make those on this hemisphere outside Canada taxable at half the effective rate applicable to those within Canada, and to do away with certain marked instances of discrimination now existing. This does not apply to those who are afloat; I am speaking about the ones who do not get that class of exemption. For instance, an army officer at Sydney is taxed at the full Canadian rate, and he is not taxable at all at St. John's, Newfoundland. They are not taxable at all overseas. We thought it would be much fairer to make this gradation. There are reasons why it is less desirable perhaps to be outside Canada, on this continent, than in Canada. We thought this was the best procedure to take.

The point is this: The man in the merchant marine to-day cannot be classified as just an ordinary sailor, simply because he works under a minister of shipping. They have certain definite rules and regulations which they must follow; they report to the manning pools and are to some extent under military discipline as applied to the navy. Furthermore, most of these boats are just as heavily armed as a corvette. These men handle a gun and are taking the greatest risks of any section of our services. Absolutely, and in the conditions they work under they have not much chance. There certainly is no glory attached to their service. Mr. Speaker, I was going to raise this question before. I think we have strained our position as an official opposition just as far as we should be asked to do. I think I have always taken a reasonable stand in facilitating the business of the house, but here we have almost an overhaul of the budget resolutions. I would have objected before, had it not been that we feel under an obligation to give the government every possible help in getting its war measures through. But now that the resolutions have been passed, I wish to make this observation. We have been placed in a most unusual position as members of the official opposition in attempting to deal with these amended resolutions as they came up, and I do not feel at the moment that we should go any farther in consenting to what is very close to irregularities. Here we are asked to give first reading to a bill which has not yet been printed and is not yet before the house.
It is done all the time.

objection for any other reason than the one I stated. But we are engaged in a war, and the people we are dealing with on the outside, many of whom are risking and may give their lives in the war, are not receiving so much consideration as we

here are asking for ourselves. The only consideration in our minds should be that in the ultimate result nothing irregular or out of order is done.

The question having been raised, I am afraid the Chair has been placed in this position, that the bill not being before the house, leave cannot be granted for its introduction unless there is unanimous consent of the house. Well, Mr. Speaker, I suppose that, having been placed in this position in connection with it, there is very little I can do in connection with the giving of consent.
