That the definition of "standard profits" be amended to provide that the "standard profits" of wholly-owned subsidiary companies incorporated in 1942 or thereafter shall not in the aggregate exceed $5,000 when the sum of the capital employed by the parent and such subsidiary companies taken together is not substantially greater than the capital employed by the parent company prior to the incorporation of such wholly-owned subsidiary companies.

I move, for the Minister of Finance, the following amendment:
That resolution No. 1 of the budget resolutions to amend the Excess Profits Tax Act be amended by striking out such resolution and substituting the following therefor:
"1. That the definition of 'standard profits' be amended to provide that the 'standard profits' of controlled subsidiary companies incorporated in the years 1940, 1941 or 1942, or thereafter shall not in the aggregate exceed $5,000 when the sum of the capital employed by the parent having the controlling interest and
Excess Projits Tax

such subsidiary companies taken together is not substantially greater than the capital employed by such parent company prior to the incorporation of such subsidiary companies:
Provided that this provision shall not apply in the case of subsidiary companies incorporated to carry out a contract negotiated by the Minister of Munitions and Supply and if such subsidiaries are in receipt of management fees or other similar compensation from the Department of Munitions and Supply."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The situation, is apparently th.is, that if a company is heavily subjected to excess profits tax, it may be profitable for the company to incorporate a controlled or wholly owned subsidiary or subsidiaries. That does not effect any reduction in the capital of the parent company, and therefore it does not have any effect on its standard profits. But it gives the subsidiary a standard .profit, even, though no more capital is employed by the parent and subsidiary than was employed by the parent company alone. The result is that the company can economize, if that is the word, on excess profits tax, and to a very considerable degree. This is designed to prevent such procedure.
The minister does not like that kind of economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I am not in favour of that type of economy. The proviso is added because there are companies which undertake work at the instance of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and such work on some occasions can be done properly only through subsidiary companies. Very often they use capital supplied by the government, or undertake work for a management fee. In that case it is not'desirable that the provision should apply.	.

Do I understand the resolution correctly when I say that one subsidiaiy will be allowed to earn 85,000, and have that as a standard profits base of the parent company, or is it just the parent company that has the $5,000 base?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is the subsidiary. If a parent company causes the incorporation of one subsidiary company, that subsidiary company can get the .benefit of the $5,000 base. But if it incorporates more than one, the total of all of them cannot be more than $5,000. But that is not the problem, really. That is not what is going on, or can go on. The companies doing this would not be interested in $5,000.
What is the evil aimed at?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The evil aimed at is that it might be $500,000 that a parent company would take. That might he improbable, but let us say $50,000 or $100,000. It would take that sum out of its own resources and cause the incorporation of a subsidiary company, and take stock. There has been no increase in capital whatsoever, and there is no reduction in the capital of the parent company. If there were, it would lower the standard of the parent company, and it would suffer. But it does not suffer at all. On the com trary it gets the benefit of the base of $50,000 or $100,000. They can go to the board of referees, as a new company, and get as standard profits the normal rate of return, which perhaps might be that of the parent company; and then just pay on any excess earned over and above that amount. And the fact is that they have saved a lot of money. If they had not aplit their business, and had kept on as a parent company, all the money they earned would be subject to 100 per cent excess profits tax. By the incorporation, of the new company, only the part that is over the new base is subject to the excess profits tax, and it is a profitable thing to do. It is the desire to provide here that . if they do not employ any more capital, they shall not get any new standard profits, except the $5,000.
The minister creates an exception for the companies which have contracts negotiated by the Minister of Munitions and Supply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

speechtext: There is no tax evasion there. If the Minister of Munitions and Supply desires that a company undertake new business; if it is for the purpose of getting production for the crown and at the instance of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and if the company will do it on these terms- perhaps undertaking it for a management fee, or something of the kind-there is no avoidance of taxation. Perhaps that is the only term on which they will undertake to work.

stantially greater to be left to the minister? Is he to be the sole judge? Is it to be a purely arbitrary decision on his part? iMr. ILSLEY: It covers the period during which the Excess Profits Tax Act has been in operation. It is clearly contrary to the spirit of the act to set up these companies; it is an obvious method of tax avoidance.
With regard to the point about "substantially," I do not see offhand why a percentage could not be selected and used instead. I think the word "substantially" occurs in the Excess Profits Tax Act, and I think some discretion is allowed the minister to say -when there is a substantial increase or decrease. But I will take into consideration the suggestion of the hon. member when the bill is being drafted.

Under that definition
would "capital" include borrowed capital as well as proprietorship capital?
I point out also that it is the intention under this resolution to go back to the years 1940, 1941 and 1942. Once again that which may have been legal at the time will become illegal, which I think we must admit is, generally speaking, a bad principle. If there is substantial tax evasion, perhaps consideration should be given, but as a general principle I think we should protest against it.
Mr. ILSLEY; The only thing that really concerns me is whether there might not be bona fide reasons apart from tax avoidance for setting up a subsidiary in those years, I will look into that and see whether there should be any exception.
My attention has been called to the fact that the tax is not affected for the years 1940 and 1941; it is incorporation in those years to which reference is made. When we come to the enactment section, this ' amendment will apply to the profits of the year 1942 and fiscal years ending therein and all subsequent
periods. We are not going back of fiscal periods ending in 1942. There is a certain element of retroactivity, but I think that is when the activity takes place. I think it is an abuse that it is quite all right to correct.
As to borrowed capital, "capital employed" is defined in the Excess Profits Tax Act and does not include borrowed money. The term is used in the first schedule, and the method by which it is computed is set out in detail in that schedule. It "shall be subject to the following deductions", and among these is the deduction of any borrowed money.

I did not know this wa,s coming up to-night. I have been following the reports of corporations and companies published from time to time in the Financial Post. I have had someone taking the companies I have discussed, in former years and comparing the profits reported with the profits made in former years. It strikes me that while individuals are to a large extent having their incomes reduced, the corporations in this country are able to maintain a good level of profits even under our Excess Profits Tax Act. Up to last week for example,' taking all the companies reporting in the Financial Post together, the profits are -3 per cent higher than for last year. I have not the detailed figures with me to-night, but I know that is the position. If individuals throughout the country paying income tax have their standards reduced, we should expect the excess profits tax would to some extent reduce the net profits of the corporations. It seems to me to emphasize the point that somehow, no matter how you tax organizations of this kind, they are able to pass that tax on to the consumer, who in this period is very largely the government.
Having said that, I wish to bring something entirely different to the attention of the minister. I received in this morning's mail a letter from a little company in Saskatchewan. The president of the company is an old-timer in the province. It is a little company of people who wrnrk cooperatively in the store. I am going to read the letter, because it strikes me that while one criticizes the excess profits tax as not being severe enough, there are occasions when perhaps it works an injustice on some persons, particularly those in a small way. The writer of this letter says:
Excess profit is supposed to be any amount now earned that exceeds the average profit for the years 1936 to 1939 inclusive. If no profit was earned in those years, the taxpayer is supposed to be allowed $5,000 as a standard profit and he has only to pay a straight income tax on any figure above the $5,000. I say that is the supposition, because in actual practice,
Excess Profits Tax

under certain circumstances, the taxpayer is mulcted for an excess profit tax even if he only makes $1,000, or say one per cent on his investment, and here is how it is done.
If the actual profits of a joint stock company do not exceed $5,000 they add on the salaries of all shareholders that are working for the company, which of course boosts the total above the $5,000 mark, and so makes the company liable to pay excess profit tax.
Of course these wages and salaries are legitimate expenses and by no stretch of the imagination could they be called profit, and there is neither rhyme nor reason in treating them as such. But that is one of the provisions of the act, which means that no matter how small our real profit may be we will always be mulcted for excess profit tax as four of our shareholders are working for the firm.
We would be pleased if you could take this matter up with those who are responsible with a view to having this obvious injustice removed.
I pass the letter over to the minister in order that he may see what there is in this complaint. If the complaint is a legitimate one, it seems that something should be done to remedy it, when three or four or five people are working together under the circumstances outlined in this letter. I pass it over to the minister because probably it is a matter of regulations.

Where a company is controlled by the employees and it is open to them to pay themselves such salaries as they wish, naturally the profits of that company may be only $2,000 or $1,000 a year. I had a case before me the other day in which a man told me his profits were $2,000, but the profits of the business before paying salaries were nearly $60,000, and two men had taken about $27,000 or $28,000 each in salary, so that there was not much profit left to the business.

I happen to know the head of this little firm, which is in a small town in Saskatchewan. I am perfectly sure the profits there would not permit of the payment of salaries which would be considered more than just an ordinary living. I think this is a matter the minister should look into. I quite agree that in cases such as the minister has mentioned, persons should not be allowed to pay themselves exorbitant salaries.
No; we do not let them do so.
I quite agree, but I think this is a case which might be looked into.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I asked the hon. gentleman a question about the first matter he mentioned. The companies that have profits after taxation -3 per cent in excess of those of the previous year are the companies whose years end when?
At the end of December. Some of the companies have not reported yet, but we have been following them in the Financial Post.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will remember that the increased excess profits tax rates came into effect in July, 1942, so that those companies, if they were calendar year companies, were subject to the higher rates only for part of the year whose operations are shown. I do not know what will be the showing of the companies when their full year's operations are under the 100 per cent amendment to the Excess Profits Tax Act. The 100 per cent amendment is not the most onerous feature of that act. The most onerous feature is the provision or combination of provisions which cuts their profits after taxation down to seventy per cent of their pre-war profits, and I shall be surprised if they show any such good record as that during the full year. There was great resiliency in business, of course, in Canada in the last two or three years; the companies made a tremendous showing even after taxation, and of course the taxation was enormous. Yesterday the hon. member for Temiscouata rose to make a point about Imperial Oil, and undoubtedly the hon. gentleman heard the figures he mentioned, $18,000,000 tax and $14,000,000 profit. That is the record of some of these companies. I do not know whether those figures are correct, but that is my recollection of what the hon. member for Temiscouata said. Then, of course, the dividends are taxed over again when they go to the individuals. I think the taxation on companies plus individuals is heavy enough.

Coming back to the
second matter mentioned by the hon. member for Kosetown-Biggar, just before I left Winnipeg in January a very similar case was, brought to my attention by a small printing firm in Winnipeg, a limited company of which practically all, if not all the shareholders, are working in the establishment and drawing wages. These employees expressed the view which has been stated already, that they understood the reasons for these provisions, which were stated by the minister a moment ago, namely, to make sure that such firms could not pay large salaries and avoid taxation. The case of- this printing company, however, was parallel to that of the store in Saskatchewan. Some members of the staff had shares, and some did not. The wages of those who had shares were computed toward the $5,000 figure. Their actual profits were very low and their wages are at trade union rates, so that they felt that this provision, the purpose of which

Excess Profits Tax
was very commendable, was working a hardship on them. The cases are almost identical, and I wish the minister would look into this one also.
I find that the letter which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar sent over to me was sent to me previously, and that case is being looked into.

That case or the whole
principle?
Some time ago I received through the mail from the House of Seagram a parcel in which I found a very beautiful volume entitled "Canada," by Stephen Leacock.
Is that all they sent you?
That is all. The hon. member for Rosedale asks if I still have the book. I have kept it until I had an opportunity to produce it in the house, but I propose to return it to-morrow.
Have you read it?

No; I have not read
it. A card was enclosed, saying, "Please accept with our compliments this copy-"

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I doubt very much if
this is in order. I have been extremely lenient, as I am sure the committee will appreciate, but we must discuss the specific item or we shall never get anywhere. I have been asked from several sections of the house to keep discussion to the resolution before the committee. I cannot see that what is being said by the hon. member has anything to do with the resolution before the committee at the present time.

I submit that the case I am discussing is an illustration of how companies are able to print publications of this kind instead of paying the money into the treasury of Canada, and apparently we have not the machinery to check up on the expenditures of these companies, so that publications of this kind can be put out and paid for by the taxpayers. I submit that my remarks are in order in protesting against an expenditure of this sort by the House of Seagram or any other company, using Canadian materials and spending their money in this way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I believe I should read again standing order 58, paragraph 2:
Speeches in committee of the whole house must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.

On the point of order,
I take it that we are discussing excess profits tax and also matters relating to standard excess profits. The hon. member for Mackenzie is trying to show that the excess profits which we ought to collect are reduced as a result of the publication of books of this description which are distributed by the thousand across Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I support your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I would say we are not discussing standard profits generally, or methods of evasion generally of standard profits. We are discussing a specific matter, which is the incorporation of subsidiary companies. That does not justify a discussion of the methods of evasion generally.

Amendment agreed to.
Resolution as amended agreed to.
2.	That where an upward adjustment of the standard profits has been made by the minister because of an increase in capital employed during the "standard period" then an adjustment downward shall be made for subsequent decreases in capital employed which have not been accompanied by an equivalent reduction in capital stock, but not to an extent greater than the said upward adjustment.
What is the effect of this resolution?

Once standard profits have been set and an allowance has been made on the setting of standard profits for capital employed, there can be no further adjustment, either upward, or downward, of the standard profits, without increase or decrease in share capital. If the standard profits have been increased owing to increased capital employed during the standard period, it is considered that if any portion of such increased capital is later withdrawn, even though there should be no reduction in share capital, we should correspondingly reduce the standard profits by the proper amount.

Resolution agreed to.
3.	That any amendment founded on the foregoing resolutions shall be deemed to have come into force at the commencement of the said act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It will be necessary to amend this resolution. The amendment reads:
That resolution No. 3 of the budget resolutions to amend the Excess Profits Tax Act be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"(3) That any amendment founded on resolution No. 1 shall apply to the profits of the year 1942 and all fiscal periods ending therein and of all subsequent periods, and that any amendment founded on resolution No. 2 shall be deemed to have come into force at the commencement of the said act."
I so move.

What does the minister mean by "the commencement of the said act"? Does that mean from royal assent?
Excess Profits Tax

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: From the beginning of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940.
Resolution 1 is retroactive to 1942 and this resolution goes back to 1940?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

This retroactive legislation is a bad thing. Surely the minister could use some foresight in drafting his resolution so that business men will not have to be going back all the time and opening closed books where there has been no deception, when what they did was legal at the time. It seems that in order to aid his collection department the minister changes any section of any act he desires, and as a result the business man does not know just where he stands.
He planned to avoid it.

I take extreme exception to what the hon. member has just said. I should like to point out to him how grossly he is in error. The business man acted according to the law at the time. Now the administration finds that there were some loopholes in it and they are going to change the act in order to make that which was legal before, illegal. If the hon. member has a different opinion, I should like to hear it.

This is done to confirm a procedure that we have been carrying out. There was some question as to whether we should have been doing so. This is to confirm our authority to continue what we have been doing.
You were doing it without authority?
Yes.

Amendment agreed to.
Resolution as. amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to move to add another resolution. This will be the same section as that which was designed to prevent evasions .under the income tax act. The amendment reads:
That the following resolution be added to the resolutions to amend the Excess Profits Tax Act:
"4. That section 15 of the said act be amended to prevent reduction or avoidance of liability to tax."
The sections in the income tax act and in the Excess Profits Tax Act are the same, and if we have this addition in the one we should have it in the other.

May I ask the minister again if it should not have been possible to have let us see these amendments before they

were finally moved. I do not wish to exaggerate the position, but I tried to emphasize it before. It is most difficult to attempt to deal with a brand new set of resolutions such as we have had here. I take it that in this particular case there is nothing serious involved, but perhaps the minister will explain just what are the underlying reasons for the new resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have a lot of sj'mpathy with the hon. member's position.
Many of us have been here for three days and we have not seen them at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no doubt that a number of amendments have been run in at the last, but that was not done in order to keep them dark. As amendments were agreed upon, I have tried to give notice of them from time to time. The hon. member for Rosedale says that some explanation is due of the Course that has been adopted this year. It is hard to give any other explanation than that people have had too much to do. Considerable *work had to be put on this budget before it was brought down and since it has been brought down, and considerable time has been spent in reading letters, listening to representations and receiving delegations. At the same time other business had to be attended to, and it was impossible to get everything in perfect shape at an early stage. Apart from one or two which were brought before the house last night and which necessitated an enormous amount of work in their preparation, these resolutions have not been very serious. Most of the changes have been changes in wording and correction of errors which were brought to the attention of the government. The normal course after a budget is brought down is to put the resolutions. Then representations are made by various classes of people and individuals who are interested in them. Then it is discovered that some amendment has to be made. That was the case this year. I suppose we would have reached this a little earlier if the budget debate had ended earlier. We would have reached this stage of tremendous concentration, asking people to work late hours and so forth, the discovery and remedying of defects in the resolutions earlier had the budget debate ended sooner. But it was impossible to do so. '
With regard to the bill, the preparation of a bill is more or less difficult. What took place last year was not desirable. The bill went through in a: great rush at the end, without very much examination by the house.

Excess Profits Tax
The finishing touches were put on the bill only the night before or two nights before it went through the house. Some of these sessions are nearly all-night sessions preparing these measures, and, as I say, my officials and those of the national revenue department are in a state of extreme fatigue. They can do just so much.
That is about the only explanation I can give of the fact that there have been numerous amendments. Everyone is oppressed by a sense of his responsibility to place on the statute books legislation that will not effect injustices. In fact,, one of the reasons why our Income War Tax Act is so complicated is that we have taken so much pains to try to iron out anomalies and prevent injustices from arising. If we were rougher and took less note of inequities, we would have a 'much simpler statute and much simpler schedules, but so much pain is taken to try to avoid these things that we have a complicated tax structure and a complicated act and a very difficult one to amend.

I shall be very brief in view of what the minister has said. First of all, I think it was the Prime Minister who made the statement that there had been a good deal of time consumed in the budget debate. But what position would the government have been in, had that debate wound up earlier? The situation that we have had to face to-day would then have had to be faced perhaps a couple of weeks ago. and the difficulties, from the point of view of the minister, would have been just that much greater. When the minister speaks about amendments to the resolutions being brought into the house, as a matter of fact most of them or at least a number of them were brought in prior to the time wljen the resolutions were discussed. That indicates that the resolutions had to be changed after having received further consideration by the department and the minister. I checked up on the time consumed in the budget debate, and I find that thirty-two government speakers, nineteen opposition, nine Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, ten Social Credit and six others took part in it. Perhaps there is no reason for either the minister or myself becoming greatly exercised over the matter; but since there has been some discussion as to holding up the budget resolutions from being considered in committee, I think it is just as w,ell that we have had this clarification of the situation that really existed in the preparation of the resolutions.

I should like to make a few observations apropos of the speech that has just been made by the Minister of Finance. He has mentioned the complicated tax structure and the amount of work that these measures impose upon the officials. I have suggested on various occasions, and I do so again to-night, that a great many of these difficulties could be ironed out if they were discussed by the banking and commerce committee. They would not need to be discussed by that committee just before the budget comes down, but I think the people of this country should have an opportunity of making their representations and airing their grievances, not before the experts of the government, but before the banking and commerce committee, where witnesses could be called and all these matters, the principles of the Income War Tax Act, the Excess Profits Tax Act and all that sort of thing, thoroughly discussed. The banking and commerce committee consists of men who were selected by the people of Canada and who are responsible to the people of Canada. Whether they are experts or not, I think that committee might very well be used to discuss principles of taxation and the taxation laws as we have them now. Then, when the next year comes round with a new budget, we would have something to go on, and the members would have some reasonable knowledge of the whole business.

I should like to endorse what the hon. member for St. Paul's has just said. After what the Minister of Finance has just said about the intricacies and the difficulties of framing a budget and the practice of last-minute considerations and reconsiderations, surely the people of Canada will get some idea of the difficulties which an opposition that is sent here for a purpose must undergo. It is utterly impossible for any member of this house, particularly a private member, to do justice to the financial considerations which are brought down by the minister, unless a committee system of some sort is adopted. It'is true that a committee system may result or appear to result in a certain delay, but we have seen what happens when the minister relies upon his professional advisers to draft certain sections. The public hears that certain taxation laws are to be changed and delegations come to Ottawa, as the minister has said, and endeavour to get the taxation arranged so that it will be practicable and fair to the people of this country. It is a travesty upon parliament that the opposition and private members of this house should be asked to pass upon the legislation which the minister brings before the house. Every self-respecting member of this house must protest
Excess Profits Tax

against being made a rubber-stamp in connection with the budget. The only possible solution is to have a committee, and that committee must also have its own independent professional advisers who will be able to give it advice from time to time, rather than have the committee rely exclusively upon advice from the government side.
Let me mention a specific case, because we are under section 15, which corresponds to section 32A. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned the case of a small corporation out in western Canada which had three or four principal proprietors, all of whom worked in the store, and who had a standard profits base of $5,000. If, in order to get what I think the hon. member who raised the question would consider a square deal, enough for those men to live on, they dissolved their corporation and formed a partnership, or if one of the members bought out the others and then hired them at reasonable salaries according to what the business would stand, that might be considered under section 32A as I read it, an evasion, or a transaction or series of transactions to reduce artificially the amount of tax. Under the resolution which we passed a little while ago and that which we are about to pass now, the treasury board could decide how much tax was being avoided; under the terms of the section they could assess and levy upon the taxpayer such tax as the treasury board might decide, and such tax shall be payable by him as in this act provided. It seems that the section which we are now considering has very far-reaching effects, and only in the hands of the department which will treat it with the utmost fairness can it be considered reasonable legislation. But we have seen in some of the provinces that the administrators do not always remain sane and sound, so that legislation should not be passed which depends upon the character of those who are to operate it.

I have just one
more observation to make in this connection. The effect of this resolution, as of the one which we passed a little while ago, seems to be this:	We pass a law, and then we pass
another law to give power to the treasury board to say that something which has been done legally is illegal. I am not a lawyer, but that is the way in which it appeals to me, and I think it -is ridiculous.

Resolution agreed to.
Resolutions reported, read the second time and concurred in.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, April 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe for the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Department of Munitions and Supply Act.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, I will not speak at
great length about this bill, but it is fitting for hon. members at times to express the opinions of their electors instead of being silent, especially when a member has proved already once or twice in his political career that he can rise to heights of eloquence and defend his own folk. Of course that is a matter of opinion, and since opinions are free, I will proceed in all freedom to say what I have to say about this measure.
The other day the debate ended1 abruptly, and I am delighted that it is resumed again. When it was adjourned I was talking of the actions of the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) when he was Minister of Finance, and even before that, and I said nothing offensive on that subject. The last words that were said by the member for Temiscouata at the time of the abrupt adjournment were that Colonel Magee was a good Canadian. But there was a state paper which was signed by the three defence ministers to the effect that there would be no patronage in the defence departments, and since the Minister of National Defence was not here the other day I must summarize in a few words the first observations I made on that dark night.
The joint declarations made by the defence ministers were to the effect that there would be no patronage in their departments, but they did not go so far as to say that there would be no patronage exercised by them in other departments. On that fateful day of February 21,	1941, I mentioned that Colonel Magee,
president of Barclays bank, a former codirector of the Minister of National Defence, and also Mr. Henry Borden, a nephew of Sir Robert Borden, the former chief of the Conservative party, had been fairly well looked after. I said nothing offensive against them; they must be very good men to have such important key positions. But what I do not understand-I may be very dull-is that, since the Department of National Defence is no more a finance department; since it was decided in the time of Mr. Dunning that the Minister of National Defence would have nothing to do with finance, would not even

Munitions and Supply Act
have the right to approve the payment of a Sam Browne, or a cap, or even a button, there has been a great transformation in that field. All financial powers were taken away from the then Minister of National Defence, who is now Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie). But now, sir, it is an altogether different matter. The Minister of National Defence is also a financial wizard, and he is the perpetual acting minister of finance. Why, I do not know, because he has not the right to approve the payment of anything. But 'he has a financial adviser who is no less a man than the president of Barclay's Bank, his former co-director. All that is linked together, but it is a very long story, and I shall try to make it short.
What goes far beyond my understanding is that Mr. Henry Borden, the noted nephew and publisher of the memoirs of the former Tory leader, a very distinguished old gentleman who is now dead, has been promoted by leaps and bounds to the high position of what has been well described as lord high executioner, the character Koko in the Mikado. Now he is chief of all priorities-a big man; and he comes from Barclay's Bank, a fine institution of which the Minister of National Defence was at the time a director. He was a good chum. And, mind you, I say nothing offensive about Mr. Borden or Mr. Magee; I am rather praising them highly. But I do not know that there has not been a little patronage, and I am wondering whether it is not because the Minister of National Defence has known those gentlemen so well, and has learned to appreciate them so much. It may be that when he was sitting with them on the board of Barclay's Bank that he thought fit to recommend them in a special manner to his colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), and tell him that he could not find in the whole country such a good and able man as Mr. Borden to be chief of priorities. It shows that there is no patronage, but it is the same thing that is done in the civil service commission. It is the merit system, which has been the guiding star of the Minister of Munitions and Supply in his choice of Mr. Henry Borden as head of the priorities branch.
And, besides that, the Department of Munitions and Supply can develop indefinitely, because it is the department of the magic carpet. It has been described in a committee of the house-but I will not insist upon that. It would be a good thing to have a comprehensive view of the coordination in that department. There are, of course, many coordinators. Do they, or do they not, coordinate? That is a very important point.
And many hon. members are under the impression that the coordination is infinitesimal. Of course there are controllers, and I know they control a lot. They are' jealous of each other. The trouble with those controllers is that they try to control each other, and naturally that leads to a certain degree of disorder, which is deplorable in such an institution. There are controllers, coordinators and what else?
We had supplied to us at the request of the former leader of the opposition a very interesting chart of the Department of Munitions and Supply. It was printed in large type so that hon. members should not ruin their eyesight in looking at it. But I know that Mr. Sheils, the deputy minister, was very proud of his chart. He had founded one of the marvels of the world, and he was exhibiting the chart to everybody. I had occasion in the house to tell the minister what I thought of the organization of his department, and I shall not repeat it. This was said a year or two ago, and I am sure it is as fresh in his mind as it is in the minds of hon. members.
Now I would have to take each name, in turn, and check it. This reminds me of children's play, and the cross-word puzzles worked by older persons. That is the best way to describe the chart of the department. And, mark you, sir, I admire the spirit and the activity of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I am sure if he were never interfered1 with by the Minister of National Defence, in connection with financial matters in his department,' and in fact its whole organization, the department would run much more ismoothly. But the Minister of National Defence, who is also hard-working, and who finds that being the head of a department is not enough, may like to put his nose into the business of his distinguished colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and give him some advice-which must always be doubtful, if not always wrong. I would ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply to be very careful about the advice given to him by the Minister of National Defence, for the very reason that that hon. gentleman has not enough time, while supervising the numerous branches of his department, to look deeply into the features of legislation and the administration of the Department of Munitions and Supply.
If the minister of that department would be good enough to give us a general idea of its organization, I would ask him kindly to tell us what is the main job done by each group of men in the little square in the big frame on that chart. He need not tell us with respect to each individual, because that would

Munitions and Supply Act
take too long. But if there is an hon. member who has that chart before him at the moment, he will understand very well what I .want to know.
We find long sentences in this bill. Apparently it is drafted according to present standards of legislation. As we know, legislation has either risen or fallen to such a degree that it is very hard for a layman to understand it. As I did not practise law for some years, I am among the group who do not understand much of the phraseology in legislation. This would be a fine occasion to poke a little fun at my humble self, and to say that I do not know what I am speaking about. But I do not pretend to have a profound mind, or to be endowed wTith the knowledge of those far-seeing statesmen who are now preparing for the post-war period.
We are in war time, and we have to do our best to help the departments as much as can be done. Hon. members may think this little, very mild criticism is uncalled for, but yesterday afternoon. I was not in the house. I went to visit an ordnance depot somewhere in. Canada-I will not say any more than that. I saw many things, an enormous number of boxes and cases, but it was in the most indescribable disorder. It may be because I am a layman, "the man on the street", that I could not realize how everything was in order. But I saw amazing things. I saw, for instance, guns that are not supposed to be moved after they are installed, but each one had four tires and four exchange tires also, and piles of tires. What surprised me also- was that four-fifths of that reserve was for other countries and only one-fifth for this country. I tell the house what I have seen. I was very well received; I express my appreciation of the officers there, but I was amazed at the way in which things were piled up. I shall surely say more about that privately to the minister. It was my duty to gO' there and inform myself. There is a great deal of good there, but there are other things that cannot be so easily approved.
I praise the minister for resuming the debate. He does it well. But with regard to his department I will ask him to take hon. members into. his confidence. I will ask him to inform the members. For a time he published extensive reports of the purchases of his department, but there was one elemedt that was lacking all the time-the element of quantum.. He was informing us that the purchases of the department have been so much food from the packers, so much this, so much that, in money, but not in quantity,

I insist on order. The war is no excuse for disorder. We need order in. this country now if'we are to have it after the war.
In the department there are many officials, very nice people. I am not complaining about them, but it takes a long time to find them and after they are found it takes a long time to get an answer.
Another thing I regret in the department is the standardization of certain precepts that should be a little more elastic. Just to-day I received a letter from one of the officials concerning the price of hair-cuts in the country. He would not change for the last two years because it was decided at the beginning. I wonder whether the Department of Munitions and Supply uses hair-cuts. I do. not know.
There is another thing I should like to bring to the attention of the minister, namely, the number of middlemen with whom any one has to deal to sell, for instance, some lumber to the department. There are some exotic people who come from nowhere, who are here getting well on the fat of the land; they are neither English, Irish, Scotch, French nor Ukrainian. The name of one was Seidel; that is not English-Canada South-wood Limited. There is another who is neither British nor French Canadian, Mr. Lustwig. There is also the International Lumber Corporation of America, which is composed of two gentlemen who come from a European country. It reminds me of a joke a friend of mind told me. He was once at Atlantic City, and he saw a store with the name "Cohen and Gentleman". He saw two men standing by and he asked one, "Are you Mr. Cohen?" He said, "No; I am Gentleman." So my friend said to the other, "You must be. Mr. Cohen," "No; I am Gentleman." Both were gentlemen, although the name was "Cohen and Gentleman". Mr. Kohen, not spelled with a "C" but with a "K", is one of the middlemen through whom the lumber producers have to deal to sell their lumber to the department. There is another, he is not British or French, Mr. Hass. Those who want to sell lumber to the department have to pass through those gates.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Will the minister give a little further explanation of this? It involves considerable sums of money.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: The original act provided that requisitions involving expenditure not exceeding $5,000 shall be signed by the minister or the deputy minister or an acting deputy minister of the department concerned, or by such other officer or officers of the department as the minister of the department may authorize. Signing officers are required for requisitions; but my hon. friend, having been a member of government, will understand that these requisitions are required to carry out a total expenditure authorized by order in council, and it is found in actual practice that the buying is broken down into so many branches that it is not practical to have a single signing officer for all expenditures over $5,000. This simply allows the minister or deputy minister to deputize others to sign requisitons up to $50,000. The minister himself must sign those for more than $50,000, as in the original act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: It is a very large jump, to ten times what it was before; that was why I asked.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: The other day I was asked by a reporter to give an interview about different matters, and I said that I did not attach much importance to the long-distance telephone bills of the department.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, this section has to do with signing authorities, and I do not think it has anything to do with expenditures.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
My point has to do with
the signing of requisitions. I know very well that in this section there is no mention of telephone bills, but it gives authority to the minister and certain officials to approve accounts, so that what I have to say is strictly in relation to that. The suggestion I am going to offer is intended to save the minister trouble.
I think I am perfectly in order in discussing telephone bills under this section, for the reason that no telephone bill may'be paid by the Department of Finance until it is certified as correct by the minister or one of the officials of the department. My suggestion is that there is nothing easier than to check longdistance telephone calls. Supposing an official in Ottawa calls his home, whether it is in Vancouver or Halifax. The telephone company has the name of the official here and the exchange number of the telephone at his home. I am not complaining about long-distance calls on official business. If a member of parliament is away from Ottawa and has to deal with a branch of the department, it is only natural for him to call the minister or one of his executives and explain his trouble. That is perfectly legitimate, and no one can complain about it, not even the leader of the opposition. If a member calls the minister or one of his executives by long-distance, in order to obtain an answer in an urgent case concerning priority, or in connection with some accident, that is perfectly legitimate; it is to save time. Therefore I suggest to the minister that he give definite instructions to the personnel of his department never to charge long-distance calls which are not made on public business, but at the same time he should give them a certain latitude in regard to real business calls. The best check is to use the co-relation that exists between the name of the caller and the exchange number of his home.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I presume that the re quisitions mentioned in the various clauses of this section have to do with all matter of supplies, office furniture, office equipment and so on?

speechtext: No, no.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

signing authority for requisitions, and I think we might very well discuss matters relating to that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: What sort of appeal is there in case of any dispute in connection with one of these cases?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: There is no appeal. Ordinarily it is a case where the contractor bogs down and requires financial assistance, which the department is not prepared to give him under his management. If the contractor can carry out his contract and finance himself; if there is no undue or inflated cost, ordinarily the situation does not arise. Where, for some reason or another, the contractor is not able to carry out his contract in an efficient manner, and an advance is needed, we usually put in a controller, so that we can be sure there will be good management to work out the advance required.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Is there any general overall policy adopted by the Department of Munitions and Supply as far as the character of these contracts is concerned? That is, is it done by tender in most cases, or is it on a 
cost-plus basis, or what is the general policy of the department with respect to ordinary contracts?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: Tenders are called wherever they can be called with any expectation of getting a proper price. If it is an article with which Canadian contractors are not familiar, it is not likely that we shall get a close price by tender. In that case various procedures are adopted for placing a contract. Sometimes there is a trial run and the cost fixed. In other cases it may be a cost plus a unit profit. It is almost never a cost plus a percentage. Our contracts are always arranged so that nothing can be gained by a contractor not using the highest efficiency and every endeavour to get production. If there is no fixed price, there is usually some incentive to the contractor to reduce costs and speed up his production.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: There are many stories, and I assume the minister must have heard some of them, about cost-plus contracts. It is thought that there is sometimes a disposition to increase certain costs in order to increase the contractor's percentage. What are the restrictions and limitations placed by the department upon such contracts so that this situation may not arise?	[DOT]

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: I just stated that we never issue contracts on a cost plus a percentage. Many contracts are issued on a cost plus a fixed amount. For instance, in the case of rifles or anything of that sort, it is always a profit of so much per unit, so many dollars per unit. The more guns that are turned out and the lower cost there is, the more profit the contractor makes; the fewer guns and the higher the cost, the smaller the profit. All of our contracts have an incentive clause of that kind, so that it works against the contractor if he does not use the highest degree of efficiency.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
Have there never been
cost plus percentage contracts?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES

The work is done on a fixed-fee basis. We estimate the cost of the job and arrange with the contractor so that he will get so many dollars for doing it. If during the

Business of the House
contract the job doubles in- size, a new amount is worked out. We never have a contract where it is so much plus a percentage. Perhaps I should not say "never," because we have 6,000 contracts, but I am sure the number would be infinitesimal.

On section 6-Power to require storage.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: This is a curious section. Are there many occasions when it is necessary for the minister to use this power.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
It has been used a great
deal. This provision was in the original act, and it is in the British act. We requisition storage quite often where a building is available, and we make an agreement that the owner will protect the property unless that provision is specifically excluded from the agreement. If we pay a fee for the use of the property, he is required to protect the property housed in the building. The original act contained a section covering storage. Subsection 2 reads:
Any persons storing munitions of war or supplies under subsection one of this section shall be liable for loss thereof or damage thereto as if he had agreed to store them for reward.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
That is not a change;
it is in the present act.

speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
What is the implication
of the words, "as if he had agreed to store them for reward"? Presumably he gets some recompense for storing them?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext: This is simply to permit the minister to use space that is available. When we need the space and a building is available, we requisition it for storage. If the price cannot be agreed upon, it is determined by the exchequer court.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO BRING ACT OF 1939 INTO CONFORMITY WITH PRESENT PRACTICES
speechtext:
I agree with the principle contained in the first subsection because it is carrying out the decentralization which I have always advocated. I do not take any responsibility for drafting this subsection. The dumping of large quantities of war materials in one point constitutes a danger to the community. There is greater risk than when the material is stored in different places. The wording of subsection 2 should be more generous to the person storing the munitions of war or supplies. There should be a different liability in the case of munitions of war, especially explosives. If, after inspection, the department is satisfied that a certain building is suitable, and if it agrees to certain compensation as rental of that building, how can the
department come afterward and complain because damage has been done to the goods? It is only fair that the individual or the company owning a building should receive compensation for the space rented. We cannot ask an individual or a company to take charge of certain war materials and supplies unless there is a particular emergency. The effect of this subsection is that if nothing is charged, the owner of the building will not be held responsible for any damage done, but if a charge is made, he will be held responsible.
A distinction should be made between war munitions and ordinary supplies. Explosives, for instance, are war munitions, and a man runs a great risk in renting his building for that purpose. I am not sure that insurance companies will insure such a building. Therefore the owner needs compensation in respect of insurance on his building.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
Mr. RALSTON moved the adjournment of the house.
May I inquire from the Prime Minister, who has just come in, what the business will be for Monday and whether he is in a position to give us some idea of what we may expect in the future?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I shall ask my colleague the Minister of National Defence who has been discussing with other members of 'the government the remaining business to make the announcement. I might add a word if necessary.

What I am giving to the house is something fairly comprehensive. I wish to say first that we plan for Monday any business which is on the order paper and, to use the words of the British North America Act, without in any way limiting the generality of the foregoing we shall probably take up the bill respecting the Department of Munitions and Supply, the city of Ottawa resolution, the federal district commission resolution, the excess profits tax bill, which I understand will certainly be ready, and I expect also the income tax bill. We may call some departments in supply. I mention Trade and Commerce, Public Works, and possibly Legislation, although not necessarily in that order.

If I may say so, there is no scarcity of work ahead. May I ask the acting leader if it is the intention of the
Business oj the House

government to proceed first with the excess profits tax bill and the income tax bill-if that is the order of procedure?	.

My hon. friend mentioned first the income tax bill and the excess profits tax bill. The excess profits tax bill will certainly be ready. I am not sure about the income tax bill, but I rather expect it will be ready. The best I can say to my hon. friend is that I will call his desire to the attention of the Minister of Finance and endeavour to see if that can be arranged.
I am not particular myself, but I understood that the government regarded those two as urgent bills.

That is right. It is simply a question whether they will be ready and whether my colleague will be ready to go on. He is anxious to proceed on Monday, because he will have to be away for a while at least on Tuesday.	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
I would say just a word subsequent to the Prime Minister's remarks.
I agree with him that we ought to get on with our war measures as soon as can conveniently be done. I think he will be in agreement with me when I say that during this session, following the government's own plan, a rather unusual procedure was adopted. Immediately after the address had been voted the budget was brought on, for reasons which are well known and with which I find no fault. But when the Prime Minister speaks about the debate taking a considerable length of time in connection with a social security committee and reconstruction, I hope he is not directing his entire remarks against those on this side of the house-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, no.

-because I think the whole house must bear its responsibility in that connection, and I do not exclude the government, because it will be well remembered that the major emphasis in the speech from the throne was laid upon social security and the committee which was to be brought into being.
In connection with any delays which have occurred in the work of the house, I suppose that under a democratic system such occasions are more or less inevitable, and I know the Prime Minister would not want to criticize those tkings too much. I put on record this evening a list of the speakers who had taken part in the budget debate, and it show's that a rather considerable majority were supporters of the government. I am not raising any question about that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was it a percentage?

No; I did not get into percentages; I just kept to straight numbers. If the Prime Minister wishes to figure that out I have no objection; he has the week-end in which to do it. But on the address, for instance, there were forty-two government speakers and twenty-one opposition speakers.
That is 50 per cent for the opposition.

That is true. But if it is a question of quality the opposition has very much the advantage.
There have been very good reasons why the situation has arisen which the Prime
Questions

Minister has described. But personally I am anxious to have the war appropriation bill brought on as quickly as possible. Having in mind, however, the fact, with reference to the radio committee which will have to be set up, that concurrence in its report was not moved last year, there may reasonably be an hour or so occupied in debate on that matter. But we are prepared to facilitate progress as much as is humanly possible. There are limitations when legislation is being dealt with, and we have a certain duty to perform. But there has been no attempt designedly to do any more than legitimately criticize the measures before us according to the best light we have.
This evening the Minister of National Defence stated that there would be a two weeks' recess. Does that mean that we shall meet again on the Thursday?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We shall adjourn on Wednesday of next week for a fortnight, and resume on Thursday the 6th of May.
